cues.speaker: male

cues.text: One shared model trains on the mixed batches. A reach-and-grasp motion looks alike on most arms.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: A small set of the target robot's own episodes fine-tunes the shared model.
cues.speaker: female

cues.speaker: male

cues.text: The image is 640 by 480 pixels. The principal point (320, 240) sits at its centre.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: A block corner sits 0.1 m right, 0.05 m down, and 0.5 m in front of the camera.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Divide X and Y by Z: 0.1 / 0.5 = 0.2 and 0.05 / 0.5 = 0.1.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Multiply by the focal length of 500 pixels: 100 and 50 pixels from the centre.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Add the principal point: u = 320 + 100 = 420 and v = 240 + 50 = 290.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Move the block to Z = 1.0 m. Every offset halves and the pixel becomes (370, 265).
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Twice as far from the camera means half as far from the image centre.
cues.speaker: male

0b4e7e1e37608f9e.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Two lenses sit 6 cm apart. This distance is the baseline. Each has a focal length of 500 pixels.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: A cup stands 0.5 m in front. Each camera sees it along its own ray.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: The left camera sees the cup at column 400. The right camera sees it at column 340.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: The difference is the disparity: 400 - 340 = 60 pixels.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Depth is f times b over d: 500 x 0.06 / 60 = 0.5 m.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Move the cup to 2.0 m. The rays turn almost parallel and the disparity drops to 15 pixels.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: The matcher is off by one pixel and reports 14. The depth becomes 2.14 m, an error of 14 cm.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: At 0.5 m the same one-pixel error gives 8 mm. Stereo error grows with the square of distance.
cues.speaker: male

ec0488784952b908.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: The robot starts at 0 m and moves at 1 m/s. We estimate its position once per second.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Predict: the motion model moves the estimate to 1.0 m. Wheel slip adds variance Q = 0.04.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Measure: the camera reports 1.3 m. Its variance R = 0.09 is larger, so it earns less trust.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: The Kalman gain is P over P plus R: 0.04 / 0.13 = 0.31.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Update: the estimate moves 31 percent of the way to the measurement, to 1.09 m.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: The variance shrinks: (1 - 0.31) x 0.04 = 0.028. Two sources beat one.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Predict again: the estimate becomes 2.09 m and the variance grows to 0.028 + 0.04 = 0.068.
cues.speaker: male

239241b5e44143f1.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: The joint starts at 0 degrees. The setpoint is 90. The error is 90 - 0 = 90.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Step 1: the P term is 45, the I term 0.9, the D term 0. Command 45.9 V.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: The joint moves to 30 degrees. The error falls to 60.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Step 2: P = 30, I = 1.5. The error fell fast, so D = 0.2 x (-300) = -60.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: The command is 30 + 1.5 - 60 = -28.5 V. The derivative term brakes the joint.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: The joint moves to 50 degrees. Error 40, P 20, I 1.9, D -40. Command -18.1 V.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Without the D term, the step-2 command is 31.5 V and the joint passes 90 and comes back.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: A person drives 100 runs of 50 steps. Every logged image shows the car near the lane centre.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Now the clone drives. At step 1 its steering is a little off: 1 cm left of centre.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: At step 2 the car is 2 cm left, a view no training image shows. The error grows.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: At step 3 it is 6 cm left. Each mistake lands the car in a stranger state.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: By step 20 the car is 40 cm left and out of the lane. This is compounding error.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: DAgger round 1: the policy drives and the person labels the correct angle at every visited state.

cues.text: After 3 rounds the dataset holds 150 extra pairs. The car stays in the lane for all 50 steps.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: The simulator runs one robot with friction 1.0 and zero motor delay.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: The policy trains for 20 minutes on one graphics card and walks in simulation.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: On the real carpet the friction is 0.6 and the motors respond 20 ms late.
cues.speaker: male

cues.speaker: female

cues.text: One update needs 4,096 x 24 = 98,304 steps. At 200,000 steps per second that is 0.5 s.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: On the carpet the real robot is one more sample from the range. The policy walks.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Work problem. An incoming message needs a destination and possibly an answer.

cues.text: Facts. Power is present; the network test failed.

cues.text: Match a rule. Both conditions of the cable-check rule are satisfied.

cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Inputs 1 and 2. Inputs are observed values, not trainable parameters.
cues.speaker: female

cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Forward: 2. Multiply weight 1 by input 2 to predict 2.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Loss: 16. Compare prediction 2 with target 6 using squared error.
cues.speaker: female

cues.speaker: male

cues.speaker: male

965d700299885541.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Split the data. Keep fitting, validation, and final testing roles distinct.
cues.speaker: female

cues.speaker: male

cues.text: New images. Keep related photographs together when creating train and test splits.

cues.text: Input signal. The example has four numerical values: 2, 2, 8, 8.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Encode. Compress or transform the signal into a latent representation.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Decode. Reconstruct an approximation: 3, 3, 7, 7.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Measure and constrain. Reconstruction error is 1; a VAE also penalises divergence from a chosen prior.
cues.speaker: male

c5c0bbbb171f67f9.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Random input. Start the generator from a sampled latent value.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Generated texture. The generator produces a candidate image.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Discriminator feedback. Compare real and generated examples under the training objective.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Alternating updates. Update both networks in turn and inspect quality and diversity separately.
cues.speaker: male

b3e18da87509bf3a.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Image with objects. A scene can contain multiple instances and categories.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Predict boxes. Return candidate locations, categories, and scores.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Match references. Compare predicted and labelled objects with a stated overlap rule.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Count errors. Track misses, duplicate detections, wrong categories, and false positives.
cues.speaker: male

8846f0714251ff04.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Input image. Preserve the spatial arrangement of pixels.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Encode context. Downsampling gathers broader contextual features.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Decode detail. Upsampling combines coarse features with skip-connected spatial information.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Pixel mask. Predict a label at each pixel and compare the resulting regions.
cues.speaker: male

ffd828e52da822ba.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Tokenise text. Split text consistently and choose any normalisation rules.

cues.text: Count vocabulary. The example gives refund 0, delivery 2, late 1.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Weight terms. Terms common across documents receive less distinctive weight.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Compare documents. Use the vectors for retrieval or a baseline classifier, then evaluate errors.
cues.speaker: male

d9a4993786b4017e.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Context examples. Collect which words occur near each other in training text.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Training objective. Word2Vec predicts local context relationships; GloVe uses co-occurrence statistics.

cues.text: Vector space. Each vocabulary word receives learned numerical coordinates.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Test a use case. Compare neighbours, ambiguity, bias, and retrieval relevance on held-out examples.
cues.speaker: male

0be0ed383fd552c7.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Token sequence. Choose a window within a sequence of words.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Context and target. Neighbours small and sleeps become inputs; cat becomes the target.

cues.text: Predict target. Convert the combined context representation into vocabulary scores.

cues.text: Update embeddings. Use the prediction error to change the embedding parameters.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Start state 0. Before the sequence, initialise the recurrent state.

cues.text: Read 0: state 1. The previous contribution decays by half.

cues.text: Prompt and state. Read delivery is and form the current recurrent state.

c8a9bf779287b3cf.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Context interaction. Attention combines information according to learned queries, keys and values.

cues.speaker: male

978c32d751182b7d.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Input sentence. Maya joined North Star Ltd.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Token labels. Each token receives a category and a boundary marker.

cues.text: Define the task. Specify the allowed categories and what to do with ambiguous requests.

cues.text: Show examples. Provide representative input/output pairs without leaking test answers.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Run held-out cases. Ask for predictions on requests not used to design the prompt.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Review errors. Count wrong categories and inspect ambiguous or unsupported outputs.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Candidate population. Represent selected items as bit vectors.

cues.text: Score and constrain. B + C has weight 5 and value 9; overweight combinations are not acceptable.

cues.text: Select and vary. Prefer useful candidates, recombine choices, and occasionally mutate them.

cues.text: Check and stop. Keep the best feasible result found within the chosen budget.

cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Target: 4.6. Combine immediate reward with discounted future value.

cues.speaker: male

78455dbdd3be7a83.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Local observations. Each robot sees its own position, goal, and available information.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Proposed actions. Both independently request the narrow aisle.

cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Measure the group. Evaluate throughput, waiting time, fairness, and collision prevention together.
cues.speaker: male

d1fb28dbac561652.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Define affected people. Identify users and people affected by the system’s decisions.

cues.text: Measure by context. Compare overall and group-level outcomes with sample sizes.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Assign accountability. Name who can review, override, correct, and stop the workflow.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Monitor after release. Recheck source changes, errors, accessibility, and consequences over time.
cues.speaker: male

347b0fc9e054cf41.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Now a person checks the work. The handler confirms the attachments belong to the same claim and checks the intake requirements.

b50a60fff127b87f.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Let's follow an example. A fictional policy clause describes a covered event and an exclusion. A member of staff needs a plain-language explanation.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Here's what the AI prepares. The draft explains the event, keeps the exclusion visible, and quotes the clause location.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Now a person checks the work. The reviewer compares the explanation with the exact policy version and checks that no promise was added.

cues.speaker: male

93b69e530edea7df.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Let's follow an example. Two fictional claims contain similar repair invoice details but different claim identifiers.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Here's what the AI prepares. The system flags a possible duplicate and links both records.

cues.text: Now a person checks the work. An investigator checks whether the records describe the same event or a legitimate repeat repair.

cues.speaker: male

5b7267ac1cdaeb8f.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Let's follow an example. A fictional encounter transcript records a symptom discussion. A speaker’s reference to “last week” is unclear.

323eace0a2b4ce98.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Let's follow an example. A fictional service directory lists a clinic’s opening hours and booking phone number. Staff need to answer a visitor’s question.

cues.text: Here's what the AI prepares. The assistant returns the matching directory entry with its last-approved date.

cues.text: Now a person checks the work. The staff member checks the location and current entry, especially if a temporary closure notice exists.

cues.speaker: male

15d6c938e5cf94cc.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Let's follow an example. A fictional clinic has weekly booking totals and a calendar of closures. A holiday week has unusually few bookings.

cues.text: Here's what the AI prepares. The forecast proposes a range of likely bookings and marks the holiday as a special condition.

cues.text: Now a person checks the work. A planner checks whether low bookings reflect low demand or fewer available appointments.

8a15291797d29c52.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Let's follow an example. A fictional product sheet says “750 ml, stainless steel, hand wash.” It makes no claim about insulation.

cues.text: Here's what the AI prepares. “A 750 ml stainless-steel bottle. Hand wash after use.”

cues.text: Now a person checks the work. The merchandiser rejects an alternative draft that says “keeps drinks cold for 24 hours.”

cues.speaker: male

2e705bcee75136f9.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Let's follow an example. A fictional shop sold 40, 42, and 41 units in ordinary weeks, then 75 during a promotion.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Here's what the AI prepares. The forecast marks the promotion separately and proposes a range for the next ordinary week.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Now a person checks the work. The buyer checks planned promotions, supplier lead time, and stockouts before selecting an order quantity.

2c214ad906bdd247.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Let's follow an example. A fictional shopper asks whether a product is available today. The assistant can search product information and a stock system.
cues.speaker: female

cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Now a person checks the work. The associate checks whether stock needs a live refresh and confirms the correct store.

cues.text: The associate gives a checked answer or offers to verify availability. A product description and a current stock count come from different sources.
cues.speaker: male

f620a7a371cac021.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: Let's follow an example. A fictional pump shows higher vibration than its recent baseline after a scheduled operating change.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Here's what the AI prepares. The system flags the change and displays the sensor trend beside operating conditions.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Now a person checks the work. The engineer checks sensor quality and whether the changed operating mode explains the reading.
cues.speaker: male

cues.speaker: male

8f597c63f9257df3.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: The key-value (KV) cache stores attention data from earlier tokens. Reusing it avoids recalculating that data at every generation step.

cues.text: A transformer updates a token’s representation through several stages. A representation is a list of numbers used by later calculations.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: The moving marker follows one teaching path. Attention mixes information across positions. The feed-forward stage transforms each position’s representation.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: In a simplified residual connection, an input value of 2 and an update of 0.5 produce 2.5. Real connections add whole vectors.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: The stages perform different jobs. Reading their order helps you locate where context is mixed and where features are transformed. The animation illustrates one block. It does not run a trained transformer, show every head, or expose a model’s reasoning.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Attention mixes information from other tokens when the model builds a representation of the current token.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: One row belongs to the selected query token. Brighter cells have larger weights. A causal mask blocks positions after that token.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: If three available tokens receive weights 0.2, 0.3, and 0.5, their contributions are mixed in those proportions. The weights sum to 1.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: A concentrated row uses a few inputs more strongly. A flat row spreads the mixture. Future-token masking prevents looking ahead during causal prediction. These are synthetic teaching scores, not attention extracted from a trained language model. A bright cell does not prove understanding or explain a decision.

5508299f1ab6f950.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: A tokenizer converts text into smaller units. This lab builds units by repeatedly merging common neighbouring character pairs.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: The merge history names the joined pair. Tokens now shows the representation after the displayed number of merges.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: If a pair occurs three times, merging those non-overlapping occurrences can replace six pieces with three. The characters remain in the same order.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Frequent fragments can need fewer tokens. Different training text can produce different merges, even for the same final sentence. This character-based demonstration is not a production tokenizer. Its count is not a provider billing estimate or a guaranteed context length.

468baa7c20047459.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: A model learns by making small changes that reduce its error. Gradient descent chooses a direction from the local slope.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: The moving point represents two adjustable numbers. Its trail records their earlier values. The loss trace shows error over time.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: On this bowl, loss = 0.5 × x² + 2 × y². At x = 2 and y = 1, loss is 4. The slope is (2, 4). A 0.1 step moves to (1.8, 0.6), where loss is 2.34.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: The step reduces error from 4 to 2.34. A larger step can help on this bowl, but another surface may require smaller steps. This is a two-parameter teaching model. A real network has many more parameters. Lower training loss alone does not prove better real-world performance.
cues.speaker: male

601fa01866a3655c.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: A language model scores possible next tokens. Sampling controls how the system chooses among them. A token is a piece of text.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Each coloured segment is a share of the next-token probability. A removed token gets zero share. Remaining shares total 100%.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Imagine three candidates with probabilities 60%, 30%, and 10%. Keeping the first two leaves 90% of the original mass. Dividing by 90% gives about 66.7% and 33.3%.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Filtering changes which outputs are possible. Temperature changes the balance between them. Neither operation checks whether an answer is true. The lab uses a fixed set of invented scores. It does not generate complete answers or measure their accuracy.
cues.speaker: male

255950a6536f112e.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: An agent workflow performs several dependent tasks. Every required task must succeed for the full workflow to succeed.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Each cumulative bar includes all earlier steps. Retries add another attempt; a fallback offers an alternative route.
cues.speaker: female

cues.text: Four independent steps that each succeed 90% of the time give 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 65.61% full-workflow success.
cues.speaker: male

cues.text: Strong individual steps can produce a weak overall process. Improve the unreliable step before adding more tasks to the chain. The model assumes independent outcomes. Missing permission or bad input can make repeated attempts fail together. Successful execution can still produce a wrong answer.
cues.speaker: male

The lab assumes comparable output sizes when using request shares. Real routing needs task-specific evaluation.

5b7303893b9aff95.voice: Ava and Andrew · synthetic teaching voices

cues.text: A timeout limits waiting for one service. An end-to-end budget limits the whole user request, including repeated attempts.

cues.text: p50 is the middle simulated latency. p99 is a slower tail value. Compare both with the budget and the hard-failure rate.
